summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the Greeks across history: the continuity of the Greek language and identity from antiquity to the present, the shift from Hellenic to Roman/Christian identity in late antiquity, and the Greek diaspora and communities around the Mediterranean and Black Seas. It also covers the origins debate over the name Danaans, notable Greek scientists and seafarers, and the religious transformation from the old Greek religion to Christianity.
one_line: Overview of the Greeks' language continuity, identity shifts from Hellenes to Romaioi, diaspora, notable figures, and religious change through late antiquity.
key_facts: The Greek language has a documented tradition from at least the 14th century BC to the present day, with a break during the Greek Dark Ages (11th to 8th century BC).
Scholars compare the continuity of the Greek language tradition to Chinese alone.
From the early centuries of the Common Era, Greeks identified as Romaioi ("Romans"), while by that time the name 'Hellenes' denoted pagans.
Anna Komnene, a 12th-century historian, used the word barbarian to describe non-Greek speakers.
Waves of emigration from Cyprus followed the Turkish invasion of Cyprus in 1974.
After the ethnic cleansing of a third of the Greek population of the island in 1974, Greek Cypriots increasingly left, especially for the Middle East.
Today more than two-thirds of the Greek population in Cyprus is urban.
In Homer's Iliad, the names Danaans (Danaoi) and Argives (Argives) designate the Greek forces opposed to the Trojans.
As of 2007, Greece had the eighth highest percentage of tertiary enrollment in the world, with higher percentages for female students than male.
Georgios Papanikolaou was the inventor of the Pap test.
John Iliopoulos received the 2007 Dirac Prize for his contributions on the physics of the charm quark.
Joseph Sifakis received the 2007 Turing Award, described as the "Nobel Prize" of Computer Science.
Christos Papadimitriou received the 2002 Knuth Prize and the 2012 Gödel Prize.
Mihalis Yannakakis received the 2005 Knuth Prize.
Until the early 20th century, Greeks were distributed across the Greek peninsula, western Asia Minor, the Black Sea coast, Cappadocia, Egypt, the Balkans, Cyprus, and Constantinople.
Cosmas Indicopleustes was a 6th century merchant and later monk who sailed to India.
Christianity's early leaders and writers, notably St Paul, were generally Greek-speaking, though none were from Greece.
Some ancient Greek religious practices remained in vogue until the end of the 4th century, and the southeastern Peloponnese remained pagan well into the 10th century AD.
